nameStory: The Compton Tortoiseshell gets its name from its angular, scalloped wing edges that resemble the beautiful mottled patterns of tortoiseshell material once used for jewelry and combs. The 'Compton' part honors a place in England where early specimens were studied, though this butterfly is actually a North American native that occasionally wanders across the Atlantic!
description: The Compton Tortoiseshell is a medium-sized butterfly with distinctively ragged, angular wing edges that look almost torn. Its wings display a rich tapestry of orange, brown, and yellow patches above, while the undersides are beautifully camouflaged in mottled grays and browns. This butterfly typically has a wingspan of about 2-3 inches and belongs to the brush-footed butterfly family, meaning its front legs are reduced and brush-like rather than used for walking.

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Wings have deeply scalloped, almost jagged edges that feel papery when touched, giving the butterfly an unmistakable 'battle-worn' appearance

idTips.label: Upper Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Bright orange and yellow patches contrast with dark brown borders, creating a patchwork quilt effect that catches sunlight beautifully

idTips.label: White Marks
idTips.description: Small white spots or comma-like marks on the wing edges stand out against the darker background, sometimes forming an L-shape

idTips.label: Underside Camouflage
idTips.description: When wings are closed, the mottled gray-brown underside looks remarkably like tree bark with a slightly fuzzy texture

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with strong, erratic bursts followed by gliding, often landing on tree trunks where it becomes nearly invisible

habitat: Compton Tortoiseshells prefer forest edges, woodland clearings, and areas near birch, aspen, and willow trees in northern New England. They're most commonly found in cooler, mountainous regions and can appear in suburban areas during their wandering phases. Look for them around sap flows on trees or rotting fruit rather than flowers.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hibernation in March-April, looking somewhat faded and worn as they search for tree sap and early moisture sources.
seasonality.summer: Fresh adults appear in mid to late summer, displaying their brightest colors as they feed and prepare for the coming winter.
seasonality.fall: Adults seek out protected spots under loose bark or in wood piles to hibernate, becoming increasingly sluggish as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Hibernating adults can occasionally be found under bark or in sheltered spots during warm winter days, though they remain mostly inactive.

funFact: Compton Tortoiseshells are famous for their incredible wandering abilities - some individuals have been found hundreds of miles from their normal range, and they've even been spotted crossing the Atlantic Ocean to show up in Europe, completely baffling scientists about how they survive such epic journeys!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Mourning Cloak, but remember that Mourning Cloaks have smooth wing edges while Compton Tortoiseshells have deeply scalloped, ragged edges. Think 'Compton = Carved edges' to remember the difference.
contextualKnowledge: This butterfly is also called the 'False Comma' because of the white marks on its wings, but it's much larger than true comma butterflies and has those distinctive jagged wing edges. Despite being called 'Compton' after an English location, this is actually a North American species that sometimes disperses to Europe.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Mourning Cloak, the Compton Tortoiseshell is smaller, has much more orange coloration, and sports those signature scalloped wing edges instead of the Mourning Cloak's smooth margins. While Mourning Cloaks are dark purplish-brown with yellow borders, Compton Tortoiseshells show bright orange patches and more complex patterning.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The mourning cloak is much larger and darker than its close relative the Compton tortoiseshell, which has more orange coloration and white patches instead of the solid yellow border.
